lesson.title: Hypothetical Situations
lesson.subtitle: Conditional -ía across verbs and polite/hypothetical expressions

hook.title: Dreaming and Planning with '-ía'
hook.content: Because every regular verb in Spanish forms the conditional by gluing **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían** onto the complete infinitive, you can instantly express hypothetical dreams: **Me gustaría vivir en Madrid** ('I would like to live in Madrid'), **Compraría una casa blanca** ('I would buy a white house'), **Iría contigo** ('I would go with you', from ir + -ía)!

pattern.title: Combining Conditional Wishes with Subjunctive 'Que'
pattern.content: What if you say 'I would like YOU to visit Madrid'? Combine **Me gustaría que** with the opposite-vowel subjunctive: **Me gustaría que visites Madrid**!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: I would like to live here

exercises.target_answer: me gustaría vivir aquí, compraría, iría, sería, ¿podrías? / ¿podría usted?
exercises.meaning: I would like to live here, I / he would buy (comprar + -ía), I / he would go (ir + -ía), it would be (ser + -ía), could you (tú) / could usted?

exercises.prompt: Build 'I / he would buy' by attaching '-ía' to the full infinitive 'comprar':
How do you say 'I would go to Madrid tomorrow' (from the infinitive ir)?
exercises.meaning: I would go to Madrid tomorrow
exercises.explanation: even two-letter ir simply glues -ía onto the infinitive: ir + ía = iría!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I would like to buy this house'
exercises.meaning: I would like to buy this house

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Me gustaría vivir en esta ciudad hermosa
exercises.target_answer: Me gustaría vivir en esta ciudad hermosa
exercises.meaning: I would like to live in this beautiful city
cues: in this beautiful city: en esta ciudad hermosa
exercises.explanation: Me gustaría vivir en esta ciudad hermosa.

summary.outcome: Form conditionals across -ar, -er, and -ir infinitives (compraría, viviría, iría, sería, me gustaría).

use_example.german: Me gustaría vivir en esta ciudad hermosa y compraría una casa aquí.
use_example.english: I would like to live in this beautiful city and I would buy a house here.

summary.takeaway: Even two-letter ir ('to go') forms its conditional regularly: ir + -ía = iría ('would go')!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next branch ([5111] The Boot-Verb Gym): master stem-changing boot verbs and -go verbs!

gustaría.english_cognate: would please (me gustaría: I would like)
gustaría.english_meaning: would please (conditional: me gustaría = I would like)
gustaría.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.
gustaría.etymology_derivation: Every Spanish conditional simply glues -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían onto the whole infinitive!

ojalá.english_meaning: hopefully, I hope that, if only (always triggers subjunctive!)
ojalá.context_translation: I hope you have a great day!
ojalá.etymology_derivation: Direct Arabic inheritance in Spanish; always triggers the subjunctive mood (tengas, venga, sea)!

vivir.etymology_derivation: Latin vīvere — English vivid, revive, survive.

comprar.etymology_derivation: Latin comparāre ('to get ready, purchase') — English compare.

ir.context_translation: I am going to go tomorrow.
ir.etymology_derivation: Latin īre ('to go', preserved in English exit 'go out' and transit 'go across')!

visitar.etymology_derivation: visitation → visitar. No preposition 'to' needed in Spanish: quiero visitar (two words where English needs three).

ciudad.etymology_derivation: Latin cīvitātem ('citizenship, city') gives English 'city' and 'civic', and Spanish ciudad.

casa.etymology_derivation: Latin casa originally meant a cottage, replacing domus in everyday Romance speech.

tener.etymology_derivation: Latin tenēre ('to hold'). While other tongues used 'have' (like French avoir), Spanish promoted 'hold' (tener) to main possession.
